problem: LLM-based robot navigation from natural language suffers from hallucination and inconsistency when instructions are ambiguous or contain unspecified user preferences; prior clarification work (e.g. CLARA) does not fit LTL-based navigation and does not retain preferences.
motivation: Human instructions often imply meaning (e.g. 'the room where I forgot my keys') or hide personal preferences ('the room I like most'). Executing these without clarification is unreliable and unsafe, so the robot must detect ambiguity, ask targeted questions, and remember preferences.
key_idea: Chain an ADA-embedding + random forest ambiguity detector, a GPT-4 clarifying-question and preference-query module with conversation memory, and an LTL translation plus graph-of-convex-sets planner to turn ambiguous instructions into verified navigation paths.
insight: A lightweight supervised classifier on text-embedding-ada-002 vectors detects ambiguity better than prompting GPT-4 (0.85 vs 0.79 few-shot, 0.69 zero-shot), so the classifier is a better gate than prompting. The disambiguation step lowers classifier-estimated ambiguity likelihood by 36.8% on average. Ambiguity is treated as user-independent while preference is user-specific, which motivates separate handling and memory only for preferences.
method: Ambiguity detector: text-embedding-ada-002 embeddings fed into a random forest (100 trees) that outputs ambiguous (1) or non-ambiguous (0), no dimensionality reduction.
Clarification/disambiguation: for ambiguous input, GPT-4 receives the sentence and environment map, generates a clarifying question, then rewrites the instruction using the user's answer.
Preference analysis: GPT-4 with the map and prior interactions detects unspecified preferences, asks the user only if unknown, and rewrites the instruction accordingly.
Conversation buffer memory: stores user preferences so they are not asked again in later interactions.
LTL translation: adopts existing GPT-4-based NL-to-LTL methods (NL2TL, Cook2LTL) to convert disambiguated instructions into LTL specifications.
Path planning: uses Kurtz & Lin's graph-of-convex-sets shortest path via convex optimization to satisfy the LTL specification.

setting.backbone: text-embedding-ada-002 + random forest (trained) for ambiguity detection; GPT-4 (frozen, prompted) for questions, preferences, and LTL translation
setting.training_data: Random forest trained on 155 self-made ambiguous statements (20 hand-written across 3 environments + 135 GPT-4 paraphrases), combined with the Gopalan et al. (3382 commands, 39 LTL) and Oh et al. (6185 commands, 343 LTL) datasets, upsampled to balance; 20 ambiguous + 20 unambiguous held out for testing
setting.observation: Text instructions plus a symbolic labeled map of locations of interest
setting.action_space: Path over labeled locations, planned as piecewise-linear trajectories in a graph of convex sets from LTL specifications
setting.simulator: Custom 2D map simulation (a single example scenario)
setting.privileged: Labeled map of locations given to GPT-4; simulated user responses

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark; only an ambiguity classification accuracy table (ADA+RF 0.85) on a custom 40-sentence test set, and a 36.8% average reduction in ambiguity likelihood shown in a figure.
results: ADA + random forest reaches 0.85 ambiguity-detection accuracy, beating few-shot GPT-4 (0.79), BERT (0.71), zero-shot GPT-4 (0.69) and CLARA (0.53). Disambiguation reduces ambiguity likelihood by 36.8% on average, and one qualitative dialog example yields a correct LTL-based navigation path.
limitations: Evaluation is tiny (40 test sentences, one qualitative navigation demo), with no navigation success metrics or standard benchmarks and no real robot.
Text-only with a symbolic labeled map; no visual input, real-time feedback, or multilingual support; user responses and dataset are self-made and not yet released.
